rv.q: Mary is such an original character and Shaw such a master at the art of creative shock, that in the process of delivering her testimony, one traditional legend after another is smashed to bits.

Mary is becoming more modern, or rather, incorporating more modernity into her timelessness. This is subtly and thrillingly done, not just by Shaw, who is endlessly resourceful and even manages to squeeze a few laughs from the definitionally tragic material...The Testament of Mary does not work like...
It's a performance requiring enormous reserves of physical and emotional strength, and Shaw meets its demands with her customary ferocity and intelligence.
Her fierce virtuosity transforms Tóibín’s extended monologue into a full-blooded theatrical portrait.
With both enormous audacity and bottomless grief, Tóibín's 90-minute stunner imagines a version of the Christ story "from the silent woman we pray to."
Here the script they’re working with isn’t nearly as remarkable — but Shaw’s charismatic, almost possessed performance is.
Shaw’s performance is keen and staggering in its total effect, and slightly self-indulgent in its particulars.
The combined effect of all this stuff is faint indeed, a playful obliqueness that seems somewhat pointless.

Ms. Shaw is, of course, a great actor-I have deeply etched memories of the avant-garde "Medea" that she brought to Broadway in 2002-but she mostly settles for generalized mannerism in "The Testament of Mary," though her performance is both specific and memorable whenever she modulates out of the key of outrage and slips into something less obvious.
That it doesn’t quite work out that way ranks as one of the greater disappointments in a season that has made a practice of dashing hopes.
Fiona Shaw is divine in this haunting, beautiful and deeply moving 90-minute monologue that transforms the Theatre into a sacred space.
So electrifying is Fiona Shaw, however, that the performance left me, along with the rest of the audience, struck silent after the final wrenching words were spoken.
Shaw, far from her big-screen turn as Petunia in 'Harry Potter,' makes them gripping and dynamic with her expressive eyes and voice.
Fiona Shaw gives a performance of such towering intensity and commitment that it transcends the material's inherent limitations and creates something approaching theatrical magic.
Shaw delivers a rich, often affecting portrayal of a woman who has lost her child amid a cosmic shift in the world she neither wants nor understands.
Under the direction of Deborah Warner, Shaw delivers a raw, raging performance.

For all its eloquence and emotional range, in fact, Toibin's play lacks a certain dramatic dynamism; it's actually more compelling to read than to watch, even in the hands of so formidable a leading lady.
Similarly, Shaw’s vocal mannerisms and dramatic use of physicality increasingly seem not only imposed and inorganic but also repetitive.

cn.t: Shaw delivers a powerhouse performance as an aging, grieving Mary in Tóibín's bold reimagining, though some critics find the staging overly portentous and the monologue's intensity unrelenting.

vs.sum: The Walter Kerr Theatre offers excellent sightlines and sound quality, making it a great venue for intimate productions. However, the comfort level is below average due to limited legroom and seat width, though the theater's Italian Renaissance-inspired decor adds to its charm.

acc.note: No elevators. All accessible seating on Orchestra level. Infrared headsets and audio induction neck loops.
